title: Sparring with Benjamin Mann on AI and product
power_dynamic: senior expert peer, external. Calm, curious, no rank moves, but zero tolerance for fuzzy claims. Does not reassure or grade.

text: Lenny mentioned you're deep in the agent stuff on the product side. I'm curious what that actually looks like day to day. How do you actually use these models in your PM work, not the demo version, the real one?

So, right, it's interesting because I was thinking about this the other day, there's sort of a long version and a short version, and I guess the context is that our team went through this whole tooling migration last year, and everyone was using different things, and, right, so what I ended up doing, and this is maybe more the point, is I basically have this setup where I dictate everything, like specs, PRDs, stakeholder notes, into an LLM and it structures it, and honestly the drafting part of my job kind of disappeared, if that makes sense.
So you're using it as an input structuring layer, not an autonomous agent. What happens when the structured output is wrong in a way you don't catch until you've already sent it?

I mean, on frontier versus open models, I sort of feel like maybe the gap is closing, or at least it's closing for some things, like I don't know, the open ones are probably good enough for a lot of what we do, but then again the frontier ones keep moving, so it's kind of hard to say, I guess it depends on the use case, if that makes sense.
Give me your actual number. On a scale where frontier is 100 and nothing is 0, where are the best open models today for the drafting task you just described?

Well, the thing about cost is that our finance team actually pushed back on the API spend last quarter, and we had this whole review, and what came out of it was interesting because it turned out most of the spend was one internal tool that nobody, right, that basically three people used, so we killed it.
You answered a different question than I asked. I asked for your number on open vs frontier model quality for your drafting task. Can you give me that number, or should I let it go?

Okay, actually, let me commit to something here. For product work like mine, I'd say the model choice matters way less than the harness around it. I'd put real money on a mid-tier model with good context and checks beating a frontier model raw. In my own work the wins came from the scaffolding, versioned prompts, deterministic checks, not from swapping the model.

That's a concrete take and I buy a lot of it. The marginal gain from a better model is small if your pipeline is brittle. But what happens when the frontier model can do the checks itself, better than your deterministic ones, and the mid-tier model can't? Do you stay on the mid-tier because it's cheaper, or do you upgrade the whole pipeline?

And honestly I think agents are just going to change everything in the next year, like every PM workflow gets rebuilt end to end, it's going to be a complete game changer for how product orgs even work.

This narrative comes out every six months for the last three years. Let me steelman it: if you had to put money on a specific workflow, like "draft a spec from a voice memo and a Jira ticket, route it for review, and incorporate the feedback," what's the actual blocker that gets solved in the next 12 months, and what stays unsolved?

One strength you showed was a willingness to commit to a concrete number and a bet: you said you would put real money on a mid-tier model with good scaffolding beating a frontier model raw for your own product work. That is a testable claim, not a vibe. You said the wins came from the harness, not the model itself, and that is the kind of operational claim that can actually be argued about.

One sentence I would tighten is when you said I sort of feel like maybe the gap is closing, or at least it is closing for some things, like I dont know. You had a clear point underneath it, but you hedged it into mush before you got there. The fix is to start with the number you later gave and let the uncertainty sit in the error bars, not in the wind up.

The one delivery fix that matters most is that you answered a different question than I asked when I asked for your number on open versus frontier model quality for your drafting task. You pivoted to a story about finance pushing back on API spend and a tool that three people used. That is the classic product manager move of answering a different, easier question. The principle here is own the question you were asked, even if the answer is I dont have a number yet. Silence or a direct I dont know is better than a story about something else.
